  "text": "Tobias went to the house after the morning service. He had stayed through the last hymn, though there had been no reason to stay and he had not sung.

The eleven posts stood straight beside the path. At the bottom, the lantern lay on its side. He left it there.

Maren's door was shut. He knocked with his knuckles, softly, as if she might be sleeping. Then he tried the latch.

The front room smelled of cold ashes. The lamp stood unlit on the sill, its chipped side toward the glass. Her father's rug lay flat. Tobias had helped carry it into the house the winter before her father died; he remembered how heavy it had been, how they had stopped halfway up the path and pretended to admire the weather.

He called her name once.

In the kitchen a cup stood upside down beside the sink. A clean cloth had been folded over the back of a chair. He touched neither.

He went out and shut the door. The latch caught. He pressed it again to be certain.

At the gate he met the woman who brought eggs on Mondays. She asked whether Maren was in.

He looked at the basket under her arm.

“Not today,” he said.

She gave him two eggs for himself. He carried them home in his coat pockets, one hand closed around each, and took the church road, though it was longer.

All the way he kept his hands still.",

  "text": "One egg had broken by the time he reached home. He found the crack with his thumb and stood in the passage, holding it above his open hand.

He cooked the other for his supper. The broken one he tipped into a saucer and set outside for the cat that sometimes came from the net sheds. In the morning the saucer was clean.

For three Mondays the woman carried eggs up to Maren's house. On the fourth she asked Tobias whether she ought to stop.

“Yes,” he said, then asked what she would do with them.

“Someone always wants eggs.”

By November the path had narrowed. Grass leaned between the eleven posts, and rain gathered in the lantern where its glass was gone. Tobias could see it from the road. He thought of turning it over before the frost, but did not go through the gate.

There were things in the house that would suffer from the damp. He knew this. Once, passing the church, he almost asked the minister who was responsible for them.

That winter he began taking the shorter road again.

One evening he stopped opposite the house. The window held the last of the daylight. He could make out the lamp on the sill, but nothing beyond it.

He stayed until a cart came along and he had to step aside. The driver lifted a hand. Tobias lifted his own.

At home he hung his coat beside the stove. Deep in the pocket, a little piece of shell caught beneath his nail.",

  "text": "He put the shell on the mantel while he fetched a needle. There was no blood. By morning he had forgotten which hand it was.

The thaw came late. Water ran beneath the snow without showing itself, and twice Tobias stepped through where the road appeared sound. He took his boots to the cobbler, who stuffed them with paper and said to come back Thursday.

In his older pair he could not walk far. He went to the shop and home, carrying what he needed in a sack.

The woman was there one morning, counting eggs into a basket lined with straw. She asked after his feet.

“It's the boots,” he said.

She put an extra egg in his sack. He began to tell her, then let her finish folding the paper.

When the road dried, someone cut the grass outside Maren's gate. The cuttings lay in a pale row along the ditch. Inside, the eleven posts stood among last year's growth.

Tobias stopped. From there he could see that the lantern had split along its bottom seam. Whatever rain fell into it would now drain away.

He went on before the shop closed.

That evening he cleared the mantel to wash it. He found two buttons, a receipt for paraffin, and the piece of shell. He swept them into his palm, then separated the buttons from the rest.

At the back door he shook the paper and shell into the ash bucket. The cat watched from beneath the step.
